posts.note: Open letter to the incoming Trump administration on PBMs and medical devices. Includes a quoted Trump forecast the author does not adopt (own_claim false). Normative 'should pass a law' advice not logged.

Republication of a July 2022 satire template about 'the next preventable mass shooting'. Template details logged as sincere expectations inside satirical framing; the closing 'meaningful change' line is inverted satire.
Personal note on drones over Brooklyn. Author explicitly says 'none of us know' what will happen; no forecast logged.
Podcast/video blurb. Event announcement (RAMHT SF 2025), a newsletter content plan, and 'soon VNS' at Fermata.
RAMHT SF 2025 promo. Panelist/demo logistics (Sanmai, MDhub.ai, GrayMatters, Nightware) folded into context; Sanmai tFUS 'still undergoing clinical trials' is present tense and not logged.
Author intro plus guest section by Matt Tucker (Nightware CEO). Tucker's forecasts logged with own_claim false; vague 'near-term initiatives that will make a lasting impact' not logged separately.
Personal post about the author's wife Carlene MacMillan and a podcast interview; no forward-looking claims.
Reflective solstice post with song lyrics; only the RAMHT SF 2025 ticket reminder is forward-looking.
Satirical Christmas poem about Elon Musk, republished; fictional framing, no sincere forecast.
Holiday thank-you to on-call clinicians; generic 'we will attend to them' promises, no forecast logged.
Announcement of the Ampa ONE-D single-day TMS pre-print (Jonathan Downar). Reported 90%+ remission is a past result; durability, SAINT comparison, and next-phase trial site claims logged.
Essay on device payment (NTAP, TCET, per diem psych units). Drug-price 'going up' claim appears three times; two logged, third noted.
Conflicts-of-interest essay. Event reminder, pharma-behavior-will-continue call, 'none likely to happen tomorrow', and a conditional ketosis claim logged.
Republished 2022 HIPAA essay. One generalization about lawmakers and one borderline implicit claim about non-HIPAA solutions logged; thought-experiment law is fiction.

statements.quote: One of the underlying themes of the newsletter and my career is that medical devices will matter in the future.
statements.context: Opening of the open letter to the incoming Trump administration. The author states his long-running thesis that medical devices (neuromodulation for psychiatric disorders) will matter in the future of healthcare.
statements.note: Broad thesis statement; restated across many posts.

statements.quote: We're going to knock out the middleman. We're going to get drug costs down at levels that nobody has ever seen before
statements.context: Quoted statement by President-Elect Donald Trump at a Mar-a-Lago news conference, reproduced by the author. Trump forecasts eliminating pharmacy benefit managers ('the middleman') and cutting drug costs. The author then argues it will be hard to do.
statements.note: Third-party forecast (Trump). Author does not adopt it; he is skeptical of execution.

statements.quote: It's gonna be hard to blow up that $500 billion+ a year industry—growing at an 8.8% CAGR—without them causing a ruckus.
statements.context: Responding to Trump's pledge to knock out the PBM middlemen, the author predicts the PBM industry (OptumRx/UnitedHealth, Express Scripts/Cigna, CVS Caremark) will resist and that dismantling it will be hard; he cites its size and growth rate.
statements.note: Implicit call that PBMs will not be easily eliminated; includes an 8.8% CAGR growth figure.

statements.quote: Just looking at antidepressant drugs alone , we can see that there are billions upon billions spent and projected to grow:
statements.context: Introducing a chart of antidepressant drug spending. The author restates a market projection that antidepressant spending (in billions) will keep growing, with PBMs collecting rebates on those drugs.
statements.note: Endorsed restatement of a chart projection; source of the projection not named in text.

statements.quote: Instead of getting into a huge fight with health plans about their PBM's, which the administration may be doing anyway, and I couldn't stop if I wanted to
statements.context: The author hedges that the incoming Trump administration may fight health plans over their PBMs regardless of his advice, while recommending it first pay for drug-preventing device treatments.
statements.note: Hedged aside inside a recommendation.

statements.quote: What if they were well because a medical device changed their brain? This is the future that I think is already here and getting better every day.
statements.context: The author claims device-based psychiatric treatment (replacing antidepressants and antipsychotics) is already here and will keep improving.
statements.note: Trend claim ('getting better every day').

statements.quote: And more is coming— like tFUS for anxiety and nVNS for PTSD and Migraine, as well as VNS for Rheumatoid Arthritis Pain.
statements.context: After a list of devices he wants Medicare to pay for (Accelerated TMS, Monarch eTNS, Nightware, PRISM EEG-neurofeedback), the author forecasts that more devices are coming: transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) for anxiety, non-invasive VNS for PTSD and migraine, and VNS for rheumatoid arthritis pain.
statements.note: Compound claim across several devices/indications; 'coming' likely means availability or clearance.

statements.quote: These treatments— and exciting psychedelic medicines !—are coming.
statements.context: Closing of the open letter: the author asserts the listed device treatments and psychedelic medicines are coming, and urges payment for them.
statements.note: Followed by normative 'We should cut out the middleman by paying for them' (not logged).

statements.quote: A child psychiatrist reflects, in advance, about the next preventable mass shooting that will rock our nation to the core.
statements.context: Subtitle of the republished 2022 satire template. The author frames the piece as written in advance of the next mass shooting, asserting another one will happen; the intro calls firearm deaths 'predictable' and notes 'now we have another'.
statements.note: Satirical framing, sincere underlying expectation. Originally written July 18, 2022; republished 2024-12-17.

statements.quote: we do know he purchased the assault rifle/s legally, as well as the hollow point bullets that caused such horrible wounds. These purchases were made despite his history of disturbing statements and threats, both online and in real life.
statements.context: Line from the fill-in-the-blank satire template for the next mass shooting: the author expects the next shooter will have bought assault rifles legally despite a history of threats.
statements.note: Template prediction inside satire; underlying claim reads as sincere expectation about the pattern of future shootings.

statements.quote: Yet again, high-capacity magazines allowed one young man/woman, between the ages of 14 and 26, to take his isolation and rage and turn it into a storm of lead, against which the innocent victims stood no chance.
statements.context: Satire template line: the author expects the next mass shooter to be aged 14-26 and to use high-capacity magazines.
statements.note: Template prediction inside satire; sincere underlying expectation.

statements.quote: A spokesperson for the NRA was reached and offered the following statement: “This is America, and the NRA staunchly supports the reduction of gun violence through the addition of more guns into the hands of more good guys.
statements.context: Satire template: the author predicts the NRA's response to the next mass shooting will call for more guns and blame mental illness.
statements.note: Fictional quote written as a prediction of institutional response; sincere underlying expectation.

statements.quote: This time, clearly, given the scope of the tragedy, it will be different, and meaningful change is definitely going to happen thanks to the actions of brave lawmakers representing this locality.
statements.context: Closing line of the satire template. Read literally it predicts meaningful gun-law change after the next shooting; the sincere reading is the inverse: lawmakers will not act.
statements.note: Inverted satire: literal claim is not the author's expectation; the sincere call is that no meaningful change will follow.

statements.quote: One little programming note: my next live-action newsletter event is in San Francisco on January 12, 2025!
statements.context: Announcement of RAMHT 2025 (Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment), the author's own conference, in San Francisco on January 12, 2025, with sponsors MDhub.ai, Sanmai, Videra Health, GrayMatters Health, Nightware, Fermata, Acacia Clinics.
statements.note: Own-event announcement; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Since I’m planning on writing about medical devices that modulate these nerves more, I figured explaining some basic science first would be a way to give my audience a two-for-one win!
statements.context: Newsletter content plan: the author says he will write more about medical devices that modulate cranial nerves (neuromodulation) after this cranial-nerve primer.
statements.note: Own-newsletter programming plan; low forecast value.

statements.quote: For treatment with nVNS, and soon VNS, feel free to request a consultation at Fermata in Brooklyn (and beyond by telehealth)
statements.context: Closing plug: Fermata (the author's Brooklyn clinic) offers non-invasive VNS now and, per the author, will soon offer VNS.
statements.note: Own-organization claim (Fermata); coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: This year, we kick off the night before the JPM conference on January 12th. The next event is in LA, which coincides with the American Psychiatric Association annual meeting!
statements.context: RAMHT 2025 schedule: SF event the night before JPM on January 12, then an LA event during the APA annual meeting. The post promises live demos from Videra Health (TDscreen), Sanmai (tFUS), GrayMatters Health (PRISM), MDhub.ai, and Nightware.
statements.note: Compound own-event announcement (two events); coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: It’s called TDscreen , and the even more advanced TDetect version is coming soon. You can sign up to use it with your patients now! Yes, it will be on display at the RAMHT SF 2025.
statements.context: Videra Health's tardive dyskinesia screening tool TDscreen; the author (an investigator on the trial) says the more advanced TDetect version is coming soon and TDscreen will be demoed at RAMHT SF 2025.
statements.note: Videra Health is an author-affiliated company; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: the next is January 12, 2025, in San Fransisco, 6-9 pm…right before JPM kicks off!
statements.context: Author's intro: the next RAMHT event is January 12, 2025 in San Francisco, 6-9 pm, before JPM.
statements.note: Restatement of the RAMHT SF 2025 announcement; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: We’re just six patients away from finalizing critical data that will strengthen our case for payers and providers.
statements.context: Guest section by Matt Tucker, CEO of Nightware, explaining the crowdfunding (Reg CF via StartEngine). Item 1 of the funding goals: complete the clinical trial, six patients from finalizing data that will strengthen the payer case.
statements.note: Guest author (Matt Tucker) claim; the author publishes it as partner content and does not restate it.

statements.quote: Insurers need proof of value. We’re delivering that proof to ensure NightWare is covered and accessible to all who need it.
statements.context: Matt Tucker's item 2 of Nightware's funding goals: build clinical and economic evidence so that insurers cover Nightware.
statements.note: Guest author claim about future insurance coverage.

statements.quote: This pilot will expand our presence in Veterans Affairs healthcare systems, directly reaching the patients who need us most.
statements.context: Matt Tucker's item 3 of Nightware's funding goals: launch the VA Pathfinder Innovation Pilot, which he says will expand Nightware's presence in VA healthcare systems.
statements.note: Guest author claim.

statements.quote: And tickets to January 12th’s event at JP Morgan Health’s (“JPM”) Opening night bash, called Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment SF 2025 , are on sale now!
statements.context: Closing reminder of the author's RAMHT SF 2025 event on January 12 during JPM.
statements.note: Restatement of the RAMHT SF 2025 announcement; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: More often than any other depression treatment I've ever seen, that depression will no longer be a problem for that person for some period of time. We don't yet know how long depression will stay at bay using this approach, because it's brand new.
statements.context: Announcing the Ampa ONE-D pre-print (Jonathan Downar): 20 TMS sessions in one day with dextroamphetamine and d-cycloserine, 90%+ remission at six weeks, no control group. The author claims treated patients' depression will be gone for some period, while flagging unknown durability.
statements.note: Ampa is an author-affiliated company (CONTROL candidate). Compound: outcome claim plus explicit uncertainty on durability.

statements.quote: Thus, for patients with acute suicidality, that approach may still prove superior.
statements.context: Comparing ONE-D's delayed response with faster protocols (Magnus Medical SAINT, HOPE-TMS, H-coil accelerated TMS, 60% remission by day five): the author hedges that 5-day accelerated approaches like SAINT may still prove superior for acutely suicidal patients.
statements.note: Hedged comparative call.

statements.quote: There is more work yet to be done, but I'm thrilled to be a clinical trial site for the next phase of the work Ampa is doing at both Fermata and Acacia clinics.
statements.context: The author states Fermata (Brooklyn) and Acacia Clinics (Sunnyvale) will be clinical trial sites for the next phase of Ampa's single-day TMS work.
statements.note: Own-organization commitment (Ampa, Fermata, Acacia); coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: The future is so close, and in it, people are suffering less pretty quickly.
statements.context: Closing line after describing the portable ONE-D stimulator: the author forecasts a near future of rapid relief from depression via single-day treatment.
statements.note: Vague optimism claim; low resolvability.

statements.quote: What happens to a drug price… if that drug price can be any price? That price is going to go up.
statements.context: Essay on why devices can't get paid while drugs can. Because Medicare Part D barred government price negotiation, the author predicts new drug prices will keep rising.
statements.note: First of three restatements of the rising-drug-price claim in this post.

statements.quote: To be blunt— drug prices are going to go up forever because they can't be negotiated down?
statements.context: Restatement: drug prices will rise forever because the government cannot negotiate them; the Inflation Reduction Act only nibbled at the edges. Later restated as 'the cost of those drugs is just going to get higher'.
statements.confidence_phrase: are going to go up forever
statements.note: Restatement; the third version ('just going to get higher') is not logged separately.

statements.quote: Using a per diem contract (paying a daily rate, not a bundle rate for the whole admission) means nothing New and Good can come to inpatient psychiatry.
statements.context: The NTAP (New Technology Add-On Payment) applies only to bundled Medicare payments; 75% of inpatient psychiatric units use per diem contracts. The author forecasts no new technology will reach inpatient psychiatry under that model.
statements.confidence_phrase: nothing New and Good can come
statements.note: Structural negative call.

statements.quote: If we don't have a path to payment by the government, and thus we won't get new technology to the market. That's the bottom line.
statements.context: Conditional forecast: without a guaranteed government payment path (NTAP inpatient, TCET outpatient), new mental-health technology will not reach the market; investors will keep favoring drugs.
statements.note: Conditional.

statements.quote: The Breakthrough Therapies Act would help solve this problem, but it hasn’t passed yet—or the similar H.R.1691 —Ensuring Patient Access to Critical Breakthrough Products Act of 2024. Again, these things need to pass a pretty dysfunctional Congress. If you ask for a solution, some of those bills will go a long way.
statements.context: The author says the Breakthrough Therapies Act or H.R.1691 (Ensuring Patient Access to Critical Breakthrough Products Act of 2024) would help device payment if passed, while noting Congress is dysfunctional.
entities: Ensuring Patient Access to Critical Breakthrough Products Act of 2024
statements.note: Conditional on passage; no call on whether the bills pass beyond 'dysfunctional Congress'.

statements.quote: I have a Event in real life with the people who inspire me at our second annual rapid-acting mental health treatment conference in San Francisco on January 12 .
statements.context: Mid-essay reminder of the author's RAMHT SF 2025 conference on January 12.
statements.note: Restatement of the RAMHT SF 2025 announcement; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: Finally, I want to remind my readers that I have an event coming up on January 12 in San Francisco. It's Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment SF 2025 .
statements.context: Event reminder for RAMHT SF 2025 on January 12; later the author says he has invited Chris Aiken (Carlat Report) to join the conference.
statements.note: Restatement of the RAMHT SF 2025 announcement; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: I don’t believe executives went to jail, however, and the drug was more profitable than the penalties, so I suspect the behavior will continue.
statements.context: After recounting the Parke-Davis/Pfizer Neurontin off-label marketing case and its criminal penalties, the author forecasts that pharmaceutical off-label marketing behavior will continue because it remains profitable.
statements.note: Broad behavioral call about pharma marketing.

statements.quote: Still, none of these things are likely to happen tomorrow. The conferences don't occur without industry support for a price we could afford.
statements.context: After listing ways physicians could resist pharma advertising (no drug reps, no TV ads, no journal ads, no conference booths), the author predicts none of these changes are likely soon because conferences and journals depend on industry money.
statements.note: Negative call on near-term change in physician exposure to pharma marketing.

statements.quote: And suppose nutritional ketosis has its early evidence in bipolar disorder replicated? In that case, it may be that changing your diet in keeping with human biology’s vicissitudes may be a potent intervention.
statements.context: Listing non-drug options: the author hedges that if early evidence for nutritional ketosis in bipolar disorder is replicated, diet may prove a potent intervention.
statements.note: Conditional and doubly hedged.

statements.quote: There is no law so invasive or punitive that lawmakers will demure if it comes to controlling either doctors or women. Preferably both.
statements.context: Republished 2022 HIPAA essay (post-Dobbs). The author generalizes that state lawmakers will pass any invasive law to control doctors or women, citing Texas defining standard of care as child abuse and abortion-ban states asserting law-enforcement access to records.
statements.note: Generalization written in 2022 and re-asserted in the 2024 republication.

statements.quote: there was almost no reason for anyone previously to engineer non-compliant solutions. Until now…let’s take a look at why
statements.context: After explaining that cash-only practices are not HIPAA covered entities, the author implies that going forward there is now reason to build non-HIPAA-compliant (more private) health records and practices.
statements.note: Borderline: implicit shift claim, not an explicit forecast.
